'''M. D. Chow''' (1878 – February 13, 1949 Shanghai), also known by the Chinese names '''Zhou Jinjue''' ({{zh|t=周今覺}}) and '''Zhou Mingda''' ({{zh|s=周明达}}), was a Chinese philatelist and mathematician. He was nicknamed the "king of Chinese [[philately]]".<ref>{{cite web |url=http://taiwantoday.tw/ct.asp?xItem=165863&ctNode=124 |title=The Story of Chinese Stamps |date=1 January 1962 |author=Chen Tse-chuan |publisher=Taiwan Today}}</ref>

==Names==
Having multiple names was the custom during the Republic era. He was also known as Zhou Meiquan ({{zh|labels=no|s=周美权}} or 周梅泉), Zhou Jinjue ({{zh|labels=no|s=周今觉}}; formerly romanised Chow Chin Tso).

==Early life==
He was born into a salt merchant family in [[Yangzhou|Yangzhou, Jiangsu]] and moved to [[Shanghai]] in 1912. He was home schooled.

==Philately==
[[File:smallone.jpg|thumb|250px|The block of four of the Small One Dollar [[Red Revenue]]s; now owned by Ding Jinsong ({{zh|labels=no|c=丁勁松}})]]
He was most noted as the founding father of Chinese philately and was crowned the King of Chinese Stamps after his acquisition of the rarest stamp, the block of four [[Red Revenue]] stamps from the original owner R. A. de Villard in 1927.<ref>Ma, Runsheng (1947.) Shanghai: ''Ma’s Illustrated Catalogue of the Stamps of China''</ref><ref name="woo">Woo, L.Y. ({{zh|labels=no|c=吳樂園}}) (1983). Taipei: ''Red Revenue Surcharges Stamp Collection'' ({{zh|labels=no|c=紅印花加蓋郵票專集}})</ref><ref name="trans">Ministry of Transportation Post Office ({{zh|labels=no|c=交通部郵政總局}}) (1984). Taipei: ''Red Revenue Surcharge, Part I'' of 2 ({{zh|labels=no|c=紅印花郵票上編}})</ref> He championed the study of the Red Revenues.<ref>Matthew Bennett, Inc. (2001) ''The "Sun" Collection of the 1897 Red Revenue Surcharge of China''. New York: Matthew Bennett, Inc.</ref>

To entertain his sick son [[Wei-Liang Chow]] in 1923, he brought home many colorful foreign stamps during his recuperation. Soon they both caught the bug and began learning and collecting stamps.<ref>''Philatelic Bulletin'', 1923, 3:3, page 27</ref> He found Chinese Philatelic Society on November 15, 1925.<ref>''Illustriertes Briefmarken Journal'', No. 2, Jan 16, 1926</ref> His bi-lingual ''Philatelic Bulletin'' won a Special Bronze Medal at the [[List of philatelic exhibitions (by country)#United States|International Philatelic Exhibition in New York]] in 1926.<ref>New York Times, ''World Stamp Show to Give 582 Awards'' 1926.04.18 retrieved 2015.09.10</ref> Chinese stamps eventually became a gold medal contender in 1927 at the [[List of philatelic exhibitions (by country)#France|Strasbourg International Exhibition]] in France.<ref name="woo"/><ref name="trans"/> He's the first Chinese to be granted a fellow of F.R.P.S.L., the [[Royal Philatelic Society London]].<ref name="woo"/><ref name="trans"/>

==Math clubs==
In Yangzhou in 1900, he created Zhixin Math Club ({{zh|labels=no|c=知新算社}}) with Bao Mofen ({{zh|labels=no|c=包墨芬}}) and Yu Yudong ({{zh|labels=no|s=余雨东}}). As one of the finest mathematicians in China, he was highly praised by Japanese scholars.<ref>Sotheby’s catalog titled ''Postage Stamps of the Far East'', April 29, 1996</ref> In the 1920s, he created [[Science Society of China]] ({{zh|labels=no|s=中国科学社}}) with Ren Hongjuan ({{zh|labels=no|s=任鸿隽}}) and Hu Mingxia ({{zh|labels=no|c=胡明夏}}), and was named co-honorary president with [[Zhang Jian (politician)|Zhang Jian]].

==Awards and honors==
His bi-lingual ''Philatelic Bulletin'' won a Special Bronze Medal at the International Philatelic Exhibition in New York in 1926.
